title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
authors: Vitor Dallabona, Lucas Friedrich, Jonas Maziero
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

infographic.key_insight: For the studied Minimum Vertex Cover instance, QAOA and FALQON follow distinct entanglement and coherence trajectories as they approach optimal solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tracking quantum resources across circuit depth can inform comparisons of optimization strategies for near-term quantum devices.
method: Apply QAOA and FALQON to Minimum Vertex Cover.
Optimize auxiliary circuits to identify closest resource-free states using the Bures metric and Uhlmann’s theorem.
Quantify entanglement and coherence without full quantum state tomography.
infographic.evidence_signal: QAOA shows an early, pronounced entanglement peak and residual coherence, while FALQON shows a lower, later entanglement peak and smoothly decreasing coherence.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one problem instance; broader generality and auxiliary-circuit optimization costs remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods

title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
authors: G. X. A. Petronilo, M. R. Araújo, Erico S. Teixeira, Clebson Cruz
abstract: Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear $\mathcal{O}(L)$ complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the $H_2$ molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below $3\times10^{-6}$ Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

infographic.key_insight: Mamba-QE replaces the Transformer in a Generative Quantum Eigensolver with a selective state space model, enabling linear-complexity operator-sequence processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture targets a sequence-processing bottleneck in molecular ground-state simulation, with scalability to larger molecules still to be demonstrated.
method: Frame ground-state search as discrete quantum-operator sequence generation.
Use a Mamba selective state space model with O(L) sequence-processing complexity.
Condition generation on molecular distance to predict potential energy surfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: On H₂ across 16 geometries, the abstract reports energy errors below 3×10⁻⁶ Ha relative to Full Configuration Interaction, within chemical accuracy and with zero variational violations.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to H₂; linear sequence-processing complexity does not establish end-to-end efficiency or accuracy for larger molecules.
infographic.paper_title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry

title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields
authors: Zhiyao Li
abstract: Matter under extreme conditions behaves as a non-equilibrium, strongly-interacting quantum system. Such systems are in the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), where their time evolution is classically intractable. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative, but present-day devices are limited in qubit count and circuit depth, so efficient formulations and algorithms are key to scaling toward experimentally relevant QCD simulations. A scalable framework is established for simulating energy loss and hadronization in 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, in which a heavy quark traverses a lattice of light quarks. Classical lattice QCD methods are translated into physics-informed circuits to prepare the interacting ground state. The evolution is run on IBM's quantum processor ibm_pittsburgh, where the charge distribution and energy loss are measured. A further study develops the quantum simulation of the fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis, a formulation that is expected to remain efficient at all gauge couplings. Digitizing the continuous gauge fields with as few as three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables with $10^{-3}$ precision. Scaling to larger systems is limited by resource overhead, which motivates truncations that preserve the relevant observables. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) exploits the hierarchy in basis-operator contributions. Demonstrated on the adiabatic preparation of the $λφ^4$ ground state on ibm_sherbrooke, SeqHT reduces circuit depth by ~30%, suppressing hardware noise in the extracted observables. All simulations in this dissertation are validated on quantum hardware against classical benchmarks. These studies advance quantum simulations of real-time QCD dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed quantum circuits and targeted truncations enable hardware demonstrations of interacting-field dynamics relevant to real-time QCD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Efficient state preparation, gauge-field digitization, and circuit-depth reduction help fit lattice field simulations onto resource-limited quantum processors.
method: Prepare interacting ground states and simulate a heavy quark traversing light quarks in 1+1D SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
Digitize fully gauge-fixed SU(2) gauge fields in a mixed basis.
Apply Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) to reduce circuit depth in λφ⁴ ground-state preparation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports hardware validation against classical benchmarks, low-energy observables reproduced to 10⁻³ precision with three qubits per plaquette, and approximately 30% circuit-depth reduction using SeqHT.
infographic.watch_item: Scaling remains limited by qubit and circuit overhead; truncations must preserve the observables of interest.
infographic.paper_title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields

title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
authors: Riccardo Molteni, Minjun Jeon, Paolo Braccia, Abhinav Deshpande, Vedran Dunjko, Liang Jiang
abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Hamiltonian embeddings encode a classical training dataset into a parameterized Hamiltonian whose approximate ground state defines a classifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports classical or quantum inference from the learned state, offering flexibility for hybrid learning workflows.
method: Encode labeled training data into a single effective Hamiltonian.
Optimize Hamiltonian parameters using efficient gradient-estimation methods.
Approximate the ground state with a quantum algorithm to obtain the classification rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports favorable generalization guarantees, conditional hardness results for efficient classical algorithms, and a demonstration on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance depends on ground-state approximation and state-representation costs; the abstract does not establish an empirical advantage over classical baselines.
infographic.paper_title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings

title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, Jose Garcia-Alonso, Juan Manuel Murillo, Antonio Brogi
abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Broker distributes a circuit’s measurement shots across heterogeneous QPUs to meet user-defined cost, latency, and fidelity requirements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its provider-agnostic execution layer helps engineers manage backend selection and shot allocation across fragmented quantum cloud platforms.
method: Express QoS constraints and objectives declaratively with QQSpec.
Profile backends using interchangeable strategies.
Plan shot allocations with MILP or nonlinear dual annealing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmark-circuit experiments on noisy simulators show feasible QoS-aware plans and improved QoS satisfaction over single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Higher-quality nonlinear allocations require more planning time, and the abstract reports simulator-based rather than real-QPU validation.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
authors: Chia-Hsien Huang, Hsi-Sheng Goan
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

infographic.key_insight: Optimal control enables simulated 12-ns controlled-Z gates between directly coupled, tunable transmons with intrinsic errors near 2×10⁻⁵ while identifying noise-resilient operating regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Smooth flux pulses and transmon-asymmetry tuning offer practical routes to balance gate speed, fidelity, and robustness while potentially reducing recalibration overhead.
method: Optimize smooth, single-shot flux pulses while accounting for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors, relaxation, and dephasing.
Model fast electronics-induced dephasing and slow 1/f flux noise using published experimental measurements.
Identify dephasing sweet spots and exploit transmon asymmetry to improve noise resilience.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 12-ns gates near an 11.6-ns theoretical speed limit, intrinsic errors around 2×10⁻⁵, and noise models calibrated against published measurements.
infographic.watch_item: The reported intrinsic error is not the total error under decoherence, and performance requires validation on experimental hardware.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
authors: Joseph Sullivan, David Amaro, Michael A. Perlin
abstract: We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

infographic.key_insight: Injecting prepared logical resource states enables addressable, parallel universal fault-tolerant operations in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture combines logical computation with error correction and could reduce resource-preparation spacetime costs relative to surface-code cultivation.
method: Flexibly concatenate small-distance, high-rate self-dual CSS codes.
Prepare CSS stabilizer resources using flag-at-origin and global magic states using concatenated cultivation.
Consume resources through Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation, requiring at most 12D_T resource states for an algorithm with T-depth D_T.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks of resource-state preparation for several two-level concatenations of H codes and the [[15,7,3]] Hamming code report at least a tenfold spacetime reduction for concatenated cultivation versus surface-code cultivation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported resource-preparation advantage does not by itself establish end-to-end hardware performance or implementation feasibility.
infographic.paper_title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes

title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

infographic.key_insight: Simulated quantum layers can improve vision-language accuracy or reduce trainable parameters, but benefits depend strongly on placement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For hybrid VLM design, layer placement matters: parameter savings do not reliably translate into lower computation or shorter training.
method: Used LLaVA-OneVision with classically simulated 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits.
Compared four quantum-layer insertion locations and four classical-component replacement locations.
Evaluated accuracy, computational cost, and robustness under six attack settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Visual Spatial Reasoning development data, insertion after the visual projector achieved 80.7% accuracy (+2.28 percentage points over classical full fine-tuning), while replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retained 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Results from classical simulation do not establish quantum-hardware advantages, broader generalization, or security gains.
infographic.paper_title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?

title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
authors: Grzegorz Czelusta, Marcin Markiewicz, Jakub Mielczarek, Artur Miroszewski
abstract: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$Φ$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Cosmos-Lab/cophi.

infographic.key_insight: COΦ maps photonic quantum operations onto qubit circuits using truncated Fock-space encodings, bridging optical and digital quantum computing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The Python compiler converts Blackbird quantum-optics programs into OpenQASM circuits, enabling digital simulation of low-photon-number optical systems.
method: Truncate each optical mode’s Fock space to a finite dimension.
Construct qubit representations of phase rotation, displacement, squeezing, and beam-splitter operations.
Provide explicit circuits for truncation dimensions N=2 and N=4.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports explicit circuit constructions and discusses benchmarking of implemented operations, but provides no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Finite Fock-space truncation limits applicability when appreciable photon-number probability lies outside the retained states.
infographic.paper_title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits

title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm
authors: Ming Zhong, Xiangyu Ren, Kangyu Zheng, Zhi Zeng, Shenggen Zheng, Shaohua Li
abstract: Selecting an effective quantum compiler configuration requires coordinated decisions over both hardware targets and compiler settings, with the ultimate goal of improving circuit execution fidelity. Existing SOTA approaches typically decompose this problem into two sequential stages: a device is chosen first, after which compiler options are tuned on that device through RL-based search. This bottom-up strategy can be fundamentally limited by its initial device decision, since a poorly matched backend may constrain the best fidelity achievable regardless of how effectively later compiler options are optimized. In contrast to classical compiler tuning, where the search space is often prohibitively large, the configuration space of quantum compilers remains manageable enough to support exhaustive search. Consequently, rather than repeatedly searching from candidate configurations, one can derive reusable configuration knowledge from offline oracle results and apply it directly to new circuits. In this paper, we introduce a top-down configuration-selection paradigm and build QuOPTBench, an exhaustively searched benchmark containing oracle configurations for 268 quantum circuits. We first study whether LLMs can directly infer suitable configurations and evaluate ten representative LLMs. The results reveal that vanilla LLMs remain far from the oracle. We then employ an LLM to extract transferable rules from sampled circuits governing configuration selection. Using these rules together with predictors trained on the enumerated configuration data of the sampled circuits, we design QuTOP, a rule-guided ML framework that performs fast configuration selection without iterative online search. Across our evaluation, the distilled rules consistently strengthen LLM-based selection, while QuTOP provides the strongest overall balance between solution quality and selection latency among the baselines.

infographic.key_insight: QuTOP replaces device-first, iterative quantum compiler tuning with top-down selection guided by reusable rules and learned predictors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Jointly considering hardware targets and compiler settings can avoid backend choices that limit execution fidelity while reducing online selection latency.
method: Build QuOPTBench by exhaustively searching configurations for 268 quantum circuits.
Use an LLM to extract transferable configuration-selection rules from sampled circuits.
Combine those rules with predictors trained on enumerated configuration data to select configurations without iterative online search.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across evaluations including ten representative LLMs, vanilla LLMs remained far from oracle performance, distilled rules improved LLM selection, and QuTOP achieved the strongest overall quality–latency balance among tested baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to unseen circuit families or changing hardware calibrations needs validation, and exhaustive offline search may become costly as configuration spaces grow.
infographic.paper_title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm

title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement of Kerr-Cat Qubits with an ATS Coupler
authors: Kerem Yurtseven, Shantanu R. Jha, Apoorva Limaye, Risav Pokhrel, Muhammad Waqar Amin
abstract: Kerr-cat qubits offer a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing by suppressing bit-flip errors exponentially, while phase-flip errors increase only linearly with the mean photon number. To maintain this protection, entangling operations must be bias-preserving, ensuring that phase-flip errors occurring during the gate do not propagate into bit-flip errors. In this paper, we propose an asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) parametric coupler to implement high-fidelity, bias-preserving entangling gates between Kerr-cat qubits. By engineering a photon-number asymmetry between the control and target modes, we enable fast gate operations that suppress non-adiabatic leakage without complex pulse shaping. Through numerical simulations of the full circuit Hamiltonian, we demonstrate a bias-preserving CX gate achieving 99.69% fidelity in the absence of photon loss for a gate duration of 50 ns. Under a single-photon loss rate of 100 kHz, our protocol yields a noise bias of 9922, exceeding the noise bias of a naive non-bias-preserving CX implementation by approximately a factor of 570. These results support the ATS coupler as a valuable building block for concatenated cat-qubit architectures.

infographic.key_insight: An asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) coupler enables fast entangling gates between Kerr-cat qubits while preserving their protection against bit-flip errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design offers a potential building block for fault-tolerant cat-qubit architectures without requiring complex pulse shaping.
method: Use an ATS parametric coupler to mediate a bias-preserving CX gate.
Engineer unequal photon numbers in control and target modes to suppress non-adiabatic leakage.
Evaluate gate performance through full circuit-Hamiltonian simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations report 99.69% CX fidelity in 50 ns without photon loss; at a single-photon loss rate of 100 kHz, the noise bias reaches 9922, approximately 570× that of a naive non-bias-preserving CX.
infographic.watch_item: The results are numerical rather than experimental, and the quoted 99.69% fidelity excludes photon loss.
infographic.paper_title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement of Kerr-Cat Qubits with an ATS Coupler

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
authors: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

infographic.key_insight: Classical Houdayer cluster updates amplify the diversity of quantum-generated maximum independent set solutions by up to 11,923×, with a median gain of 24.3×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Post-processing can extract more distinct optimal configurations—and sometimes larger independent sets—from Rydberg-array measurements without additional quantum sampling.
method: Seed solution sets with measurements from QuEra’s Aquila analog quantum device.
Apply classical Houdayer cluster updates to expand the solution sets.
Measure diversity gains and manifold coverage using known exact ground-state degeneracies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 43 problem instances, post-processing recovered a median 21% of the ground-state manifold and provably recovered the entire manifold for six instances.
infographic.watch_item: The method is non-ergodic, so complete ground-state manifold coverage is not guaranteed.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates

title: Buffer-Qubit-Based Quantum Circuit Allocation Method Against Crosstalk Attacks
authors: Haruki Nakayama, Satoyuki Tsukano, Satoshi Kono, Keita Matsumoto, Toshio Mori, Takumi Oikawa
abstract: Quantum Multi-Programming (QMP) enables the simultaneous execution of quantum circuits from multiple users on a single quantum chip in cloud quantum computing services. However, QMP is vulnerable to crosstalk attacks, in which a malicious user deliberately induces crosstalk to disrupt other users' computations. As a countermeasure, prior work has proposed the use of buffer qubits, which remain idle and are allocated between quantum circuits to suppress the effect of crosstalk. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, such countermeasures have not been publicly reported in production quantum cloud software. In this paper, we extend the QMP of OQTOPUS, open-source software that is already in production use for operating real quantum computers, with a buffer-qubit-based circuit allocation method. Experiments on a real device characterize the attack effect in terms of energy relaxation and dephasing, showing that observable degradation appears in dephasing characteristics of qubits adjacent to the attacker circuit. Based on this result, we release the proposed method as part of OQTOPUS and confirm that the buffer qubits are correctly reserved around the allocated circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Reserving idle buffer qubits between users’ circuits offers a practical defense against crosstalk attacks during quantum multi-programming.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method adds crosstalk-aware circuit allocation to OQTOPUS, open-source software already used to operate real quantum computers.
method: Characterize attack-induced energy relaxation and dephasing on a real quantum device.
Extend OQTOPUS allocation to reserve idle buffer qubits around circuits.
Verify that the allocator correctly reserves the buffer qubits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Real-device experiments found observable degradation in the dephasing characteristics of qubits adjacent to the attacker circuit; allocation checks confirmed correct buffer reservation.
infographic.watch_item: Buffer qubits consume chip capacity, and the abstract does not quantify their attack-mitigation benefit or throughput cost.
infographic.paper_title: Buffer-Qubit-Based Quantum Circuit Allocation Method Against Crosstalk Attacks

title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
authors: Neereja M. Sundaresan, Nicholas Cotaj, Yadav Prasad Kandel, Eric Lewandowski, Christian Robert Longton, Yves Martin
abstract: Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: Four 80 cm superconducting interconnects linked two 120-qubit processors, enabling high-fidelity state transfer and cross-module entangling gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Perpendicular cable installation and post-mount indium bonding offer a practical route toward denser connections between modular quantum processors.
method: Connect lattice qubits through frequency-tunable L-qubits, RF-SQUID couplers, and superconducting aluminum coax.
Use interconnect modes near 5 GHz for relay-based quantum state transfer.
Implement distant CZ gates and generate simultaneous Bell pairs over two adjacent links.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four links, mean state-transfer fidelity was 99.00% and mean distant-CZ fidelity was 94.75%; best-link results were 99.29 ± 0.07% and 96.42 ± 0.28%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Scaling beyond four links remains unproven, and cross-module CZ fidelity trails state-transfer fidelity.
infographic.paper_title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors

title: Fast Template Matching for Quantum Circuits Using Hypergraph
authors: Xin Hong, Jintao Yu, Runhong He, Shenggang Ying, Sanjiang Li, Mingsheng Ying
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a key step toward the efficient execution of quantum algorithms. Template matching has emerged as one of the dominant approaches for simplifying quantum circuits, yet it confronts the intrinsic challenge of accommodating gate commutativity. The state-of-the-art template-matching algorithm relies on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation. While this DAG-based technique handles gate commutativity satisfactorily, it fails to preserve the local connectivity inherent to quantum circuits, thereby leading to relatively high matching complexity. In this paper, we introduce a hypergraph representation (HG), a commutativity-aware representation that collapses commuting gates into a single super-node while retaining all local connectivity. This enables matches to be extended locally without revisiting the rest of the circuit, with incremental updates limited to the immediate neighborhood. Experimental results demonstrate that our HG matcher achieves 11--606x speed-up over the DAG-based implementation in Qiskit (Iten et al., 2022) on both random and arithmetic benchmarks, while maintaining the same optimization quality. The acceleration increases with circuit size, confirming that preserving locality and connectivity is the key to scalable quantum circuit optimisation.

infographic.key_insight: A commutativity-aware hypergraph representation accelerates quantum circuit template matching by preserving local connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster template matching can reduce quantum circuit optimization time without sacrificing optimization quality on the evaluated benchmarks.
method: Collapse commuting gates into single hypergraph super-nodes.
Preserve circuit connectivity to extend matches locally.
Restrict incremental updates to the immediate neighborhood.
infographic.evidence_signal: On random and arithmetic benchmarks, the HG matcher achieved 11–606× speedups over Qiskit's DAG-based implementation with the same optimization quality; acceleration increased with circuit size.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested benchmark families and the overhead of constructing the hypergraph require further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Fast Template Matching for Quantum Circuits Using Hypergraph

title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication
authors: Aleksei Kodukhov
abstract: The resource theory of coherence quantifies the quantum properties of states and their role in quantum information processing. Extending coherence theory to ensembles, the natural objects in quantum communication, remains an active research direction, with their operational potential still being explored. In this work, we establish a maximally coherent ensemble in every finite dimension: the continuous ensemble of pure states distributed according to the normalized Haar measure attains the tight upper bound on basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence. We then prove that ensemble coherence bounds the effective informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states. Finally, for the qubit B92 QKD protocol, we show that the coherence of Alice's ensemble upper-bounds the secret key rate in the asymptotic regime. These results give ensemble coherence a quantitative operational meaning in quantum communication and cryptography

infographic.key_insight: The Haar-distributed ensemble of pure states maximizes basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence in every finite dimension, linking coherence to quantum communication limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ensemble coherence provides theoretical upper bounds for postselection-based information gains and asymptotic secret key rates in qubit B92 quantum key distribution.
method: Prove that the normalized Haar ensemble attains the tight coherence upper bound.
Bound the informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states.
Bound the asymptotic B92 secret key rate using Alice’s ensemble coherence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical proofs and protocol-specific bounds, not numerical benchmarks or hardware experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The operational bounds address restricted settings and do not establish achievable performance under finite-key or noisy-device conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication

title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
authors: Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Roeland ter Hoeven, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order parity constraints can improve QAOA success probabilities beyond resolving hardware connectivity limits, apparently by accelerating correlation propagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Parity-based QAOA offers a promising route to better optimization on sparse quantum hardware using parameters trained on smaller instances.
method: Apply selected parity transformations to Signed Max-Cut on 3-regular graphs.
Classically optimize QAOA parameters on training instances with up to 14 vertices.
Transfer parameters to larger instances on IBM Heron processors and apply error mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In tests up to 40 vertices, parity-based QAOA with error mitigation found optimal solutions for every tested 40-vertex instance, while conventional QAOA failed under the same conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the tested instances; broader generalization and the hardware overhead of higher-order operators require further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization

title: Shot Allocation Strategies in Debugging Quantum Circuits
authors: Era Thaqi, Coco Gong, Margaret Martonosi
abstract: Debugging quantum programs remains challenging due to the nature of quantum measurement. As quantum algorithms and systems scale, it is increasingly crucial to develop rigorous debugging and verification approaches. Statistical assertion-based debugging validates quantum program behavior through repeated circuit execution and statistical hypothesis testing, but existing frameworks treat shot count as a fixed input parameter, leaving the problem of optimal shot allocation across multiple mid-circuit assertions unexplored. To improve debugging efficiency by making better use of given shot counts, this paper proposes and evaluates four shot allocation strategies within the QDB quantum debugger implemented within the CUDA-Q framework. These allocation approaches: equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement, use statistical approaches to test whether qubits have expected state characteristics at different points in execution. We evaluate these allocation strategies on different circuits, under both noise-free and depolarizing noise conditions. We show how adaptive strategies use shots efficiently by concentrating them on assertions with high uncertainty. This substantially reduces total shot usage while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive shot allocation can reduce quantum debugging executions by focusing measurements on uncertain assertions while maintaining comparable confidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Allocating shots across mid-circuit assertions can make statistical debugging more resource-efficient as quantum programs scale.
method: Implement four allocation strategies in the CUDA-Q-based QDB debugger.
Compare equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement.
Use repeated circuit executions and statistical hypothesis tests to check expected qubit-state characteristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations across multiple circuits under noise-free and depolarizing-noise conditions report substantially lower total shot usage with adaptive strategies, though the abstract provides no numerical savings.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits under broader hardware noise models and on physical quantum devices are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Shot Allocation Strategies in Debugging Quantum Circuits

title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
authors: John Zaris, Wes Johnson, Krishna Balaji Sogathur, Athreya Shankar, John J. Bollinger, Allison L. Carter
abstract: Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.

infographic.key_insight: A semiclassical molecular dynamics framework models EIT cooling in Penning-trap ion crystals, including efficient axial-mode cooling in simulated 3D crystals with up to 500 ions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can guide cooling-protocol optimization for trapped-ion quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.
method: Evolve internal quantum states alongside classical ion motion to calculate instantaneous EIT laser forces.
Analyze planar drumhead-mode cooling with planar ion motion and finite laser beam width.
Engineer 3D mode spectra to enable sympathetic cooling of low-frequency E×B modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors validate single-ion cooling rates against fully quantum simulations and demonstrate axial-mode cooling numerically in 3D crystals containing up to 500 ions.
infographic.watch_item: Single-ion validation does not establish the semiclassical model’s accuracy for all many-ion regimes or experimental conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap

title: CoDecoder: Make Quantum Decoders Up to 100x Faster and Even More Accurate
authors: Yicheng Guang, Yuliang Xiong, Xun Gao, Yueqi Chen
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers need fast and accurate error decoding. We present CoDecoder, a small neural frontend that composes with an existing decoder to improve accuracy and reduce mean decoding time. It predicts each shot's logical outcome, retains confident predictions and routes the remaining shots to the unchanged fallback. A logical-operator-aware output head scores shifted logical operators, combining equivalent logical lines on surface codes and deciding logical qubits jointly on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Fused GPU inference and efficient routing reduce the overhead paid on every shot. In registered tests under circuit-level noise, composition reduces failures by 6.4-31.4% relative to correlated matching on surface codes of distance 7-17 and by 22-50% relative to full-DEM Relay-BP on two BB codes, with 2.3-124-fold speed-ups across these comparisons. With our re-implementations of the neural decoder Cascade, composition reduces decoding time in all four settings. A joint decision of both decoders on the routed shots keeps this speed and makes the composition more accurate than Cascade in all four, with 14-18% fewer failures on the [[72,12,6]] code. On the [[72,12,6]] BB code, a conventional head with independent logical outputs fails 3.8-5.0 times as often as our joint class score under matched training conditions. Per-shot analysis shows how composition gains accuracy. On retained shots, the frontend corrects more fallback errors than it introduces, even when it is less accurate overall.

infographic.key_insight: CoDecoder pairs a small neural frontend with an unchanged quantum error decoder to improve accuracy while accelerating mean decoding time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Confidence-based routing and fused GPU inference offer a practical way to accelerate existing quantum error-correction pipelines without replacing their decoders.
method: Predict each shot’s logical outcome, retain confident predictions, and route uncertain shots to a fallback decoder.
Use logical-operator-aware scoring: combine equivalent logical lines for surface codes and jointly decide logical qubits for BB codes.
Reduce per-shot overhead with fused GPU inference and efficient routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Registered circuit-level-noise tests on distance-7–17 surface codes and two BB codes reported 6.4–50% fewer failures and 2.3–124× speed-ups versus the respective conventional fallback decoders.
infographic.watch_item: Reported speed-ups concern mean decoding time; real-time deployment also needs validation of tail latency and routing overhead on target hardware.
infographic.paper_title: CoDecoder: Make Quantum Decoders Up to 100x Faster and Even More Accurate
